summary_html: A **parent/guardian/child requests help** without a substantiated allegation. FFPSA created a federal pathway for **prevention services** to avert removal and stabilize families before a case escalates.
authority_html: - **Family First Prevention Services Act (2018)** — prevention services, kinship support; shifts upstream from removal to support

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of Reena D.
key_cases.holding: The court held that when a parent moves to terminate a guardianship over a minor that the parent originally established by consent, the guardian opposing termination bears the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence; the trial court's use of a lower standard required vacatur and remand.
key_cases.relevance: Parents who voluntarily place a child with a relative through a consensual guardianship retain a constitutionally weighted right to have the child returned.
key_cases.quote: we now hold that the clear and convincing standard of proof applies to the guardian’s burden of proof in a proceeding to terminate a guardianship established by consent

key_cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of Brittany S.
key_cases.holding: Applying the three-part due process balancing test, the court held the State Constitution did not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent petitioning to terminate a guardianship over her daughter, and that the probate court did not unsustainably exercise its discretion in declining to appoint counsel.
key_cases.relevance: A parent who asks the court to undo a guardianship and regain her child proceeds without any constitutional entitlement to appointed counsel.
key_cases.quote: based upon our analysis of the three-prong balancing test, we hold that the State Constitution does not require that counsel be appointed to represent Tammy G.

key_cases.holding: On habeas corpus, the court vacated a consent order that had stripped a non-offending mother of custody, holding that a parent entering a RSA 169-C consent order waives important constitutional rights and that the State must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the parent understood the consequences and consented voluntarily and intelligently; the matter was remanded for an adjudicatory hearing.
key_cases.relevance: A parent who calls for help can become a respondent, which is precisely the risk the court's informed-consent requirement is designed to check.
key_cases.quote: the parent in an abuse and neglect proceeding who enters into a consent order is waiving critically important constitutional rights

state_agency.hotline: 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only) or 603-271-6562; DCYF Central Intake is staffed 24 hours a day, including weekends and holidays

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 169-C:29
Physicians, surgeons, county medical examiners, psychiatrists, residents, interns
Registered nurses and hospital personnel (admission, examination, care and treatment)
Teachers, school officials, school nurses, school counselors
Social workers, day care workers, and any other child or foster care workers
reporting_details: New Hampshire is a universal-reporter state: RSA 169-C:29 lists physicians, dentists, psychologists, registered nurses and hospital personnel, teachers, school officials and school nurses, social workers, day care and other child or foster care workers, law enforcement officials and clergy, and closes with “any other person having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected,” all of whom “shall report the same in accordance with this chapter.” RSA 169-C:30 sets the route and the form: an oral report “shall be made immediately by telephone or otherwise, and followed within 48 hours by a report in writing, if so requested, to the department” — the Department of Health and Human Services, which takes reports through the DCYF Central Intake Unit at 603-271-6562 or 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only), staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays.
